   Explicit catastrophic-cut rule: If cutting here would (a) leave the left side as an apparent assertion that a negator, modal, or scope-changing phrase on the right would reverse or materially change, (b) separate a verb from its required complement/object/particle, or (c) interrupt a completing prepositional/time/path phrase or the final element(s) of an enumerated predicate, then treat this cut as very poor. Concretely: raise contra near 1.0 and set cohesion very low so target ≈ 0. Do not rely on punctuation alone.

- Judge whether essential argument structure, attachment, or scope relations cross the cut so separately translated pieces would fail to compose. Common risks: splitting predicate from object/complement, detaching a head noun from required modifiers/possessives, breaking a verb+particle or multiword predicate, forcing an attachment decision without disambiguating material, or detaching quantifiers/negation. Estimate cohesion as a 0–100 fidelity percentage for the joined, separately translated pieces.

   Referential-isolation guidance: If the cut cleanly isolates a referential unit (a title/role phrase or a proper name) so both sides contain their heads and are independently interpretable, raise cohesion—such cuts often translate well separately. Test: would each side read as a self-contained referent without the other? If yes, score the cut comparatively high.
